item.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
item.dc:creator: Ben Brubaker
item.description:
When links in a communication network go down, messages can get routed in a loop. Computer scientists now know that four simple network structures are to blame.

The post Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’ first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed. item.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
item.dc:creator: Ben Brubaker
item.description:
By injecting “thoughts” directly into large language models, researchers are trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection.

The post New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
What’s on your mind right now? You can probably answer this question without thinking too hard about it. Being aware of our own thought processes — a capacity called introspection — seems to come naturally to us. Yet among philosophers and psychologists, introspection is a subject of active debate. item.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
item.dc:creator: John Pavlus
item.description:
Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable.

The post He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. item.dc:creator: Natalie Wolchover
item.description:

item.title: As AI Closed In on ‘Unique Games’ Proof, Researchers Raced to Beat the Machines
item.dc:creator: Ben Brubaker
item.description:
In the shadow of a rumored AI proof of one of the biggest problems in their field, three computer scientists rushed to publish their own milestone result.

item.content:encoded:
On the morning of September 11, 2026, Dor Minzer received a text message from a friend asking whether he was close to settling one of the most famous open questions in theoretical computer science.
